text: It's certainly among the most pressing, because it affects everything else, from food supplies to migration. That said, I wouldn't call it the only one, since poverty and conflict cause immediate suffering that can't wait. What makes climate change special is its irreversibility. Once certain thresholds are crossed, there's no going back, which is why the next decade is so critical.

questions.question: Is climate change the biggest problem facing the world today?

text: I'd say so, as they've historically produced the bulk of the emissions and have the resources to invest in cleaner technology. It seems only fair that they help developing countries leapfrog polluting industries rather than repeat the same mistakes. Of course, poorer nations also need to take responsibility for their own policies. But in terms of who has the capacity and the greater share of the blame, the answer is fairly clear to me.

questions.question: Should wealthy countries pay more to tackle environmental problems?

text: To a degree, yes. When enough people stop buying a product, companies take notice, as we've seen with single-use plastics. The catch is that individual choices are often overstated, since a handful of corporations are responsible for most emissions. So I'd argue consumers should do their bit but also vote and campaign for stricter regulation, because that's where the real change happens.

questions.question: Do you think consumers can really make a difference to the environment?

text: It's changed dramatically. A few decades ago, environmental concerns were seen as a niche interest, whereas nowadays they feature in school curricula, business strategies and election campaigns. The shift is partly down to visible evidence, like extreme weather, and partly to younger generations who simply won't tolerate inaction. The challenge now is turning that awareness into measurable action, which is where progress is still slower than it should be.
